cards.source_text: More than 400 endangered animal and plant species could face accelerated extinction after the Donald Trump administration’s decision to rescind a rule that has protected old-growth forests for more than two decades. According to a new report from the Center for Biological Diversity, the rollback of the Bill Clinton-era “roadless rule” could put 7.4m acres (3m hectares) of endangered-species habitat and nearly 1,800 miles (2,900km) of protected rivers and streams at risk, while opening more than 45m acres of national forests to roads, drilling and logging. The Trump administration moved last week to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule, citing “outdated restrictions [that] have kept tens of millions of forested acres off-limits to the very treatments that improve forest health and reduce wildfire risk to our communities”. Conservationists have criticized the decision. “Our national forests are home to some of America’s most iconic animals, from grizzlies to hellbenders. These forests provide clean drinking water to countless communities. Bulldozing more roads through them will mean dirtier water, fragmented wildlife habitat and greater wildfire risk,” said Randi Spivak, public lands policy director at the Center for Biological Diversity. At-risk species include grizzly bears and gray wolves in the Rocky Mountains, wild salmon in the Pacific north-west and Alaska, Mexican spotted owls and Gila trout in the south-west, as well as rare butterflies and wildflowers nationwide, according to the report. In the Rocky Mountains, 9.7m acres of roadless areas are at risk, including 2.9m acres of critical habitat and nearly 11,000 miles of streams home to 21 imperiled plant and animal species. Montana’s roadless areas also protect watersheds supplying drinking water to communities in Bozeman, the Flathead valley and the Seeley-Swan valley, the report found. In Alaska, the rollback threatens wild salmon in the 9.3m-acre Tongass national forest, which produces more wild salmon than any other national forest. The region’s $1bn-a-year commercial and sport fishing economy which accounts for one in 10 jobs in south-east Alaska may also be affected, the report noted. The Tongass also supplies drinking water to more than a dozen communities, including Sitka, where about 9,000 people rely on the Blue Lake Reservoir. cards.source_text: - A family of Siraya activists in Taiwan is a major driving force behind the revival of their ancestral language — more than a hundred years after it was last spoken. - The work to revitalize the Siraya language, which began more than 20 years ago, helped secure the community’s legal recognition as Taiwan’s 17th Indigenous group. - The story of the Siraya language’s revitalization began as a love story between Siraya activist Uma Talavan and Filipino musician Edgar Macapili. - While she could not understand a Dutch missionary’s Siraya translation of the Gospel of Matthew, her husband recognized similarities between the Siraya language and his mother tongue, Bisaya, both of which belong to the Austronesian language family. TAINAN, Taiwan — Since she was old enough to understand it, Uma Talavan has known she belongs to the Indigenous Siraya people. She knew almost nothing of her ethnicity, however, the identity of which was dissolved by centuries of forced assimilation, save for a handful of words her parents used to speak. In search of “who she is,” as she puts it, the Siraya activist decided to bring her language back to life nearly 200 years after it died out. “Language is an extremely important part of a people’s soul,” she says. “It lets us know the past and connect it to the present.” Her work to revitalize the Siraya language, which began more than 20 years ago, helped secure the community’s legal recognition as Taiwan’s 17th Indigenous group. Uma Talavan, her activist father Wan Cheng-hsiung, also known as Cheng-hiong Talavan, and other members of the community traveled from Tainan to Taipei to attend a ceremony announcing the recognition on July 30. The Siraya, one of Taiwan’s Austronesian-speaking Indigenous peoples, are the largest of the Pingpu groups, the peoples who have traditionally inhabited the island’s lowland plains and coastal areas. When the Dutch arrived in southern Taiwan in the 17th century, the Siraya were the first people they came into contact with. The story of the Siraya language’s revival begins as a love story. In 1992, Uma Talavan met her future husband, Edgar Macapili, during a stay in the Philippines. Both musicians, they grew close playing music together at a local church. After settling in Taiwan, Macapili wanted to help his wife reclaim her lost identity. Uma Talavan and her father got hold of a copy of the Gospel of Matthew translated into Siraya by a Dutch missionary during the Dutch colonial period from 1624 to 1662.
cards.source_title: Siraya language, deemed ‘extinct’ over a century ago, finds its voice again in Taiwan

cards.source_text: It’s hard to imagine that the space-crazed general public needed any help getting worked up about astronauts and NASA in the early ’60s. Perhaps the wild popularity of space-related imagery was in part what motivated NASA administrator James Webb to create the NASA Art Program in 1962. Although the program’s handpicked artists weren’t edited or censored in any way, they were briefed on how NASA hoped to be represented, and which emotions their creations were meant to capture—the excitement and uncertainty of exploring these frontiers. NASA was also careful to collect everything the artists produced while participating in the program, from sketches to finished work. In turn, the artists received unprecedented access to launch sites, key personnel, and major events such as Project Mercury and the Apollo 11 Mission. Hundreds of artists, including Andy Warhol, Norman Rockwell, and Laurie Anderson, have brought their unique sensibilities to the project. (Find NASA-inspired art by Warhol and Rockwell above.) (And hey, no shame if you mistakenly assumed Warhol’s 1987 Moonwalk 1 was created as a promo for MTV…) Jamie Wyeth’s 1964 watercolor Gemini Launch Pad includes a humble bicycle, the means by which technicians traveled back and forth between the launch pad and the reinforced-concrete blockhouse where they worked. Photographer Annie Leibovitz offers two views of NASA’s first female pilot and commander, Eileen Collins—with and without helmet. Postage stamp designer, Paul Calle, one of the inaugural group of participating artists, produced a stamp commemorating the Gemini 4 space capsule in celebration of NASA’s 9th anniversary. When the Apollo 11 astronauts suited up prior to blastoff on July 16, 1969, Calle was the only artist present. His quickly rendered felt-tip marker sketches lend a backstage element to the heroic iconography surrounding astronauts Armstrong, Aldrin and Collins. One of the items they carried with them on their journey was the engraved printing plate of Calle’s 1967 commemorative stamp. They hand-canceled a proof aboard the flight, on the assumption that post offices might be hard to come by on the moon. cards.source_text: It doesn’t quite ring true to call David Bowie a rock star. Ziggy Stardust, the neon synthetic-clad alien alter ego he both created and retired in the early seventies, was, of course, rock stardom outlandishly personified. But then, that was the concept of what turned out to be just one of many personae he deliberately crafted throughout the course of his career. That career was in music, primarily, but looking back on it today, more than a decade after Bowie’s death, it looks more like his medium was culture itself. That’s underscored by his interviews, clips from a variety of which appear in the new video above from YouTube channel T&H Inspiration. Most of T&H’s most popular videos add visuals to speeches by the popularizer of Eastern philosophy Alan Watts, who’s been featured here on Open Culture before. He and Bowie had more in common than it may seem at first, beginning with an Englishness that remained thoroughgoing no matter how far out they ventured into the world. Though Watts’ interest in Buddhism hardly needs stating, it’s worth remembering that he chose to be ordained as an Episcopalian priest rather than as a Buddhist monk. The young Bowie, for his part, very nearly took the latter path, studying under the late Lama Chime Rinpoche, who eventually told him he’d be better off going into the music business. Bowie did so, of course, but with a new “sense of transience and change, which actually became fundamental to my life and my approach to it,” as he put it decades later. That sense manifests even in his early work, but embracing and even pursuing impermanence — the impermanence of sounds, of fashions, of hit records, of life itself — also kept him from getting mired in the irrelevance or auto-kitsch that threatens every superstar. Given the belief that nothing lasts forever, “looking for the source of one’s own being becomes much more important,” as does attempting artistic or intellectual challenges at the very edge of one’s abilities. Alan Watts would probably have agreed. The bigger question is, did he ever hear “Changes”? cards.source_text: Every four years, with the reliability of a reelection campaign, Interpol emerge with a new album that sounds remarkably like Interpol. They’re not the kind of band to wade through a murky psychedelia morass for an album-length fuck-you to casual fans, à la MGMT, or douse a long-awaited comeback LP in chintzy pop textures and copious Auto-Tune, like the Strokes just did. When Interpol make a record, they’re all business, and their business is being Interpol, brooding hooks and well-pressed suits and all. They may tweak the formula—the post-punk atmospherics, the alluringly charismatic baritone belonging to Paul Banks, the cryptic lyrics that connote dark emotions but are agile enough to be repurposed for goth tattoos or goofy memes. But they don’t toss it away. That reliability means you can count on them for consistency—aside from the dismal self-titled record, they’ve never made a bad one—but also means it can be tough to differentiate one post-Carlos Interpol album from another. Let’s see: There was the course-correction comeback that reintroduced Interpol as a three-piece, with Banks on bass. There was the surprisingly raw Dave Fridmann production that yielded some strong singles as the band settled into legacy status. There was the remotely written one that, uh, also had a bunch of Interpol songs on it. Now, after hunkering down with another new collaborator (prolific pop producer Andrew Wyatt, not to be confused with rock-dinosaur whisperer Andrew Watt) in their semi-estranged hometown of New York, Interpol return with another scheduled reset. No score yet, be the first to add. By all early signs, This Mirror Weighs a Ton promised a rebirth. It’s Interpol’s first album for Partisan, the thriving indie label that has lately attracted high-profile talent like Beth Orton and PJ Harvey. It’s their first to feature longtime touring bassist Brad Truax, now promoted to an official member. Early press included intriguing mentions of strings, woodwinds, and “experimental sound design” introduced by Wyatt. And its title track, released as a single, was surely the band’s most interesting song in more than a decade: Grainy and haunted, full of wobbly drum loops and gaseous synth clouds, it has a minimalist momentum and a command of empty space that gives Banks’ dour voice newfound authority. cards.source_text: Philosophy at Dundee Saved—In Part, For Now (guest post) “A small programme with a large international reach has bucked the trend of closures across the arts and humanities.” Over the summer, administration of the University of Dundee announced a plan to cut costs by, among other things, no longer offering students the option of majoring in philosophy. A campaign was launched to save the philosophy program there, and a petition in support of it garnered close to 6000 signatories. As a result of the petition, statements from academic organizations, and the efforts of faculty and students, philosophy at Dundee will continue, as the Philosophy Team at Dundee explains in the following guest post. Thanks to Oisin Keohane for keeping us informed. A Statement from the Philosophy Team at the University of Dundee Philosophy at Dundee will continue. Three joint honours degrees—Art and Philosophy, English and Philosophy, and Philosophy and Psychology—will carry on recruiting, and our plans to develop proposals for new undergraduate and postgraduate qualifications in Philosophy and AI have been approved, with support on record from Luciano Floridi and Shannon Vallor. Neither of those things were on the table in June when the proposal to suspend all named philosophy degrees was first announced. The ground shifted because of you. Nearly 6,000 people have signed our petition, including academics at 450 universities in 51 countries, from Harvard to Tokyo, Sydney to Stellenbosch. A small programme with a large international reach has bucked the trend of closures across the arts and humanities. The picture is not all good. The University still intends to suspend single honours Philosophy and multiple joint honours degrees, including Philosophy and Politics, Philosophy and Film, and History and Philosophy, without providing evidence of any clear financial rationale or assessment of the risks. Moreover, Philosophy staff remain at risk of redundancy, and the University is still seeking 154 cuts (in addition to the hundreds they made last year). We want to thank the people who made the difference. As well as Floridi and Vallor, Jack Reynolds and Katrina Mitcheson wrote personally to the University’s management. cards.source_text: Careful with those Accusations Academia is in turmoil regarding partially or wholly AI-written research. AI-written work is being submitted to journals, but it isn’t clear how much. Publisher, journal, university, and department policies are emerging and fluctuating. Technology develops, rendering recently enacted policies ambiguous, vague, or subject to unintended loopholes. With everything in flux, it’s impossible for norms to develop. There is no general sense of whether and what kind and what degree of AI use by authors is acceptable. Different policies across different institutions means that what may be problematic AI use in one place is acceptable AI use in another, and vice versa. Into this chaos steps forward the vigilantes. The vigilantes have always been there, but now they are newly armed and emboldened. In the everchanging and never ending race between the technology of deployment and the technology of detection, the latter seems to have a temporary lead in the form of Pangram. You can feed a text into Pangram and it will tell you its analysis of whether it is AI generated, and if so, what percentage of it is AI generated. Pangram claims to have a remarkably high detection and low false-positive rates, and cites studies by third parties to support these claims. Yet I have seen plenty of posts by friends and colleagues across social media showing false positives with some of their own work. So user beware. That said, even if Pangram’s claims about its accuracy are correct, it won’t always be helpful to simply know that a text is “AI generated.” This is because there are two further problems. The first problem is ambiguity about what “N% AI generated” means. cards.source_text: The first recreational alligator hunt in Louisiana in more than half a century is about to commence in the swamps of that state, with up to 5,000 hopeful trappers facing strict rules in order to snare a reptile. The state’s fish and wildlife commission banned alligator hunting in 1962 to allow the species to recover after decades of unregulated killings for meat and hides dropped numbers there to below 100,000. Now, with the population above an estimated 3 million in the wild, Louisiana is issuing public permits to licensed hunters for a month-long season beginning 1 October, across eight zones statewide. Although alligator hunting has taken place since an outright 10-year ban ended in 1972, it had been restricted to tightly regulated commercial harvesting, making this the first time the public has been able to legally snare for fun or sport a creature embedded in Louisiana’s culture and history. “Louisiana now has a robust alligator resource capable of providing sustainable recreational harvest opportunities to Louisiana residents without negatively impacting a highly valuable commercial industry that provides more than $250m annually to Louisiana’s economy,” the Louisiana department of wildlife and fisheries (LWF) said in a statement accompanying details of the hunt. Applicants have until Monday to enter a lottery for up to two per person of 5,000 tags that will allow them to hunt an alligator, with state residents paying $25 and visitors $150 for each zone they visit, on top of a $50 application fee. The hunt has been designated strictly non-commercial, meaning that those who trap one cannot sell the meat or skin. Applicants must already possess a basic hunting license issued by LWF, and are restricted to hook and line trapping, meaning they cannot use poles or other methods favored by poachers. Firearms can only be used to kill captured alligators, not for shooting free-swimming reptiles. The hunt brings Louisiana broadly into line with Florida, another state that said its conservation programs allowed alligator numbers to recover to the point where recreational hunting is permitted. Florida introduced a similarly regulated statewide program in 1988.

Did the cover grab you, were you swayed by the quotes on the front, or did you just happen to spot it on an appealing table as you walked into the shop? Did you think about all the nudges that led you to that decision – by the publisher, the bookseller or that person you follow on Insta? The reality is that our reading choices are directed and massaged at every turn. “It’s all about the art of persuasion,” says Philip Gwyn Jones, who was a publisher for more than 30 years and is now a literary agent. And who are the persuaders? They’re the booksellers, the supermarket stock buyers, the publishing houses and their ranks of marketers and publicists. And, more recently, persuasion often comes from BookTokers and online influencers, social media videos, podcasts and Instagram posts. How is all this changing publishing? We all judge books to some extent by their covers, but did you know how much thought goes into finding just the right cover, colour, font and design? cards.source_text: The protagonist of Meg Mason’s new book, the follow-up to the 2020 tragicomedy Sorrow and Bliss, is an invisible woman. She might well be standing there but you won’t notice her. She’s a techie at literary festivals – the person who shuffles up to a famous writer a few minutes before their event and apologetically slides a microphone cable down their shirt while they’re making small talk with the chair or accepting a bottle of room-temperature mineral water from an anxious publicist. No man is a hero to his valet, and no writer is a hero to the technical staff lurking in the wings of a venue. Mason’s opening pages present a teasing but not quite libellous series of cameos from real writers: George Saunders deciding at an inconsiderately late stage to insist on swapping his headset for a lapel mic; Ann Patchett being frosty with a fan; Mick Herron accidentally stepping on someone’s foot and not apologising. Sophie lurks in the wings of her own life, too. She likes her job but she has much to be sad about. Not long ago, her husband brought their relationship to an end with oafish callousness (she was in the shower; he didn’t bother to take his earbuds out while he delivered the news), and with it her hope of becoming a mother. Now her beloved books are in storage in the garage of her old house and she’s living alone in a dingy rental flat owned by her husband: “The water in Sophie’s glass tasted like pipes. She felt very tired … The coffee table was actually a cable spool with ‘12 AWG’ spray-painted on the drum.” Mason’s prose is wan and witty, handling the admixture of pathos and bathos well; and her sinuous sentences capture the wavering movements of thought with less fuss and more laughs than, say, Virginia Woolf. As a bookish person, and one inhabiting a lightly metafictional narrative, Sophie is glumly aware of her literary analogues. There’s “a lot of sad girl fiction” on her Kindle. “Eleanor Oliphant,” she reflects. “That was the worst. cards.source_text: Listen to this essay 20 minute listen Here is something we have never quite said out loud: for a significant portion of the world’s women, hunger is not a temporary state. It is a cognitive condition. It flows beneath everything: the meeting, the conversation, the stream of thought that almost ran its course before something more insistent pulled it back. For many of us, the state of hunger was present since we were old enough to understand that our bodies were under review. I was 11. I was sitting beside a swimming pool that summer, the one before middle school started, trying to follow a conversation I kept losing. I had decided, with the particular certainty children sometimes develop about the rules of the world they are entering, that I would eat as little as possible before sixth grade. The plan involved a sleeve of SnackWell’s cookies per day: fat-free, engineered to taste like cardboard, manufactured specifically for women and girls who had been told that fat was the enemy and desire was something to be managed rather than answered. The SnackWell’s cookie was itself a cultural artefact, a product designed to help women comply with an instruction they had already internalised. It did not quiet the hunger, because hunger is not a preference. It is biology doing what biology does when a body is not fed, sending signals that push everything else aside. During the day, we swam, lay on the concrete, and talked about the coming year. My attention kept sliding away from the conversation. A thought would begin and dissolve into the same insistent loop: how long until dinner, how little I could manage when it arrived, whether anyone had noticed what my body was doing without my permission. I remember listening to a teammate tell a long story and realising I had not heard most of it. Something louder had taken the space the story needed. By the end of the week, my swimsuit hung loose at the shoulders. On the first day back at school, a friend’s mother stopped at the sight of me, looked me over the way you assess a renovation that has come out well, and said I had a ‘new figure’. cards.source_text: A Vocabulary for the Future is a series by the Centre de Cultura Contemporània de Barcelona in which notable thinkers reflect on a word of their choosing and are paired with filmmakers who give their writing a visual interpretation. Together, they invite viewers to see familiar language anew, in the hope of laying the groundwork for a better tomorrow. In this instalment, the American theoretical physicist and feminist theorist Karen Barad muses on the nature of touch. Drawing partly on their essay ‘On Touching—The Inhuman That Therefore I Am’ (2012), Barad begins with a puzzle from classical physics: touch, strictly speaking, never happens, since what we feel as contact is only electromagnetic repulsion between atoms that never actually meet. Turning to quantum field theory, they reframe the question entirely. If matter has no stable, self-contained identity – if it is entangled with other matter from the very start – then touch is not a failed meeting between separate bodies, but something already constitutive of what matter is. Paired with visuals by the Barcelona-based digital artist Blanca Rego, the result is a mesmerising set of images that, alongside Barad’s words, turn something as ordinary as touch into a doorway into the deepest questions in physics and philosophy.

Inside, his wife Rosa and I shot hungry looks at his empty hands. Once again, the Caquetá River surrendered no fish. I was only two weeks into my fieldwork with the Andoque people in southern Colombia, and my eyes zigzagged in confusion between the two septuagenarian spouses. What did a dolphin have to do with anything? Rosa explained: ‘Derode had left baits by the river, and it seems a dolphin had stolen the fish that had gotten hooked in them.’ Derode nodded. The fishing had been poor ever since my arrival, and as Rosa cooked lunch from the rice and lentils I had brought from the city – the ‘White People’s Food’ – she reminisced with her husband about times when the river had been generous. She recalled how her grandfather had once hauled in an almost legendary catch by throwing poisonous plants into the shallow stream and asphyxiating the fish in great numbers. Among this enormous catch was a dolphin. Of course, she added, as if it needed no explanation, her grandfather did not eat it. ‘Why not eat the dolphin?’ I asked. The Andoque were accomplished hunters and fishermen, and there was almost no walking, swimming, crawling or flying creature that they wouldn’t relish, if they could catch it. ‘Because dolphins are people,’ Rosa said, matter-of-factly. ‘Besides, their meat smells terrible.’ Dolphins were not simply people, she went on, they were bad people, shapeshifters. Her father had once warned her never to accept the advances of unknown men while bathing at the river. As handsome as they may seem, he had said, they may be dolphins in disguise. Those reckless enough to fall for their charms would soon grow feverish, drift into madness and hallucinations, and ultimately die. No cure would save them. Look what happened upriver, Rosa said. She then told a story about a strikingly handsome man and a stunning woman who walked into a riverside bar in some village one night. Where their first three LPs hedged the band’s heroic chops behind ramshackle song structures and slovenly production, post-comeback albums like 2009’s Farm and 2012’s I Bet on Sky buttoned the flannel a bit, mirroring the cleaner, more streamlined sound of their ’90s output, which was mostly J Mascis’ work. By domesticating the Big Muff-induced guitar feedback and leaning into longer songs and the occasional touches of prog, they proved that a bona fide classic-rock trio had been hiding beneath the surface all along. But that polish sometimes gave way to the excessively quirky aimlessness that marked 1997’s Hand It Over before Mascis put Dinosaur Jr. on hiatus. Their last album, 2021’s Sweep It Into Space, maintained the band’s high floor for consistently catchy alt-rock, but its tidy stabs at Kurt Vile-assisted psychedelia sometimes strayed a bit too far from the band’s core of slacker disorder. On There Near, Dinosaur correct course by shedding any self-seriousness they’ve accrued over the past two decades, and instead wallowing happily in the muck of their formative years. Tracked with the same vintage amplifier used on their homemade debut album, the new material is the messiest and most blown-out music they’ve made this side of the millennium. It’s not quite as filth-caked as, say, Bug, but the effortlessness of it recalls the earlier era, prizing poppy melody and immediate self-expression over grandiosity. The best-loved Dinosaur Jr. records intensify the contrast between Mascis’ sheepish vocal demeanor and the raw transparency of the band’s playing, and those two elements are back in optimal sync here. Yet James’ fifth solo album and first in eight years both plays into and thwarts expectations, his boundless voice suggesting it is, in fact, possible to hit capacity. Wielding an array of his wheelhouse sounds with acuity and warmth, James returns with an album whose maybe-goofy-maybe-pensive title allows him to dance between world-weariness and renewed awe, resulting in his best work in a decade. During something of an unofficial hiatus, James was busy with solo material. With much of the sketches destined for unrealized film scores, they sat untouched until James revisited them in the fall of last year. No score yet, be the first to add. Publisher, journal, university, and department policies are emerging and fluctuating. Technology develops, rendering recently enacted policies ambiguous, vague, or subject to unintended loopholes. With everything in flux, it’s impossible for norms to develop. There is no general sense of whether and what kind and what degree of AI use by authors is acceptable. Different policies across different institutions means that what may be problematic AI use in one place is acceptable AI use in another, and vice versa. Into this chaos steps forward the vigilantes. The vigilantes have always been there, but now they are newly armed and emboldened. items.summary: From cover design to shelf placement and influencer partnerships … how publishers will persuade you to buy their books this autumn Think about the last book you bought. How did you choose it? Was it from a recommendation, a review, a TikTok video? Did the cover grab you, were you swayed by the quotes on the front, or did you just happen to spot it on an appealing table as you walked into the shop? Did you think about all the nudges that led you to that decision – by the publisher, the bookseller or that person you follow on Insta? The reality is that our reading choices are directed and massaged at every turn. “It’s all about the art of persuasion,” says Philip Gwyn Jones, who was a publisher for more than 30 years and is now a literary agent. And who are the persuaders? They’re the booksellers, the supermarket stock buyers, the publishing houses and their ranks of marketers and publicists. items.title: Sophie, Standing There by Meg Mason review – a tale of literary obsession, with cameos from real-life authors
items.summary: A heartbroken woman becomes fixated on a famous writer in this witty, touching follow-up to Sorrow and Bliss The protagonist of Meg Mason’s new book, the follow-up to the 2020 tragicomedy Sorrow and Bliss , is an invisible woman. She might well be standing there but you won’t notice her. She’s a techie at literary festivals – the person who shuffles up to a famous writer a few minutes before their event and apologetically slides a microphone cable down their shirt while they’re making small talk with the chair or accepting a bottle of room-temperature mineral water from an anxious publicist. No man is a hero to his valet, and no writer is a hero to the technical staff lurking in the wings of a venue. Mason’s opening pages present a teasing but not quite libellous series of cameos from real writers: George Saunders deciding at an inconsiderately late stage to insist on swapping his headset for a lapel mic; Ann Patchett being frosty with a fan; Mick Herron accidentally stepping on someone’s foot and not apologising. items.title: Trump rollback of US forest protections could accelerate extinction of 400 endangered species
items.summary: Decision to rescind ‘roadless rule’ opens more than 45m acres of national forests to roads, drilling and logging More than 400 endangered animal and plant species could face accelerated extinction after the Donald Trump administration’s decision to rescind a rule that has protected old-growth forests for more than two decades. According to a new report from the Center for Biological Diversity, the rollback of the Bill Clinton-era “roadless rule” could put 7.4m acres (3m hectares) of endangered-species habitat and nearly 1,800 miles (2,900km) of protected rivers and streams at risk, while opening more than 45m acres of national forests to roads, drilling and logging.
